title: The Shift
author: Stuart Jr., Dave
summary: Dave Stuart Jr. follows his earlier post on the impossible list of things teachers feel expected to do by offering a way to reframe it. He proposes replacing that long list with a single-item list: promote the long-term flourishing of young people. Both lists are never finished, but the first grinds teachers down toward countdown thinking, while the second makes unfinished work natural. He argues that meetings, clubs, tests, grades and classroom logistics are not the point, and that much of what drives the first list is fear of looking bad and ego rather than student benefit. Counterintuitively, the shift makes him better at the first list, because it helps him decide what to skip, what to satisfice and what deserves most of his effort. He presents this as a practical discipline for serving well in hard circumstances rather than naive optimism.
points: Replacing a sprawling to-do list with the single purpose of long-term student flourishing changes how the never-finished nature of teaching feels, from oppressive to expected.
Much of the pressure of the long list comes from fear of reputation and ego, which are not the purposes of school.
The shift is practical, not just inspirational: it lets a teacher sort tasks into skip, satisfice, and invest-most-effort.
Meetings, clubs, tests and grades are subordinate means, and are worth doing only insofar as they connect to student flourishing.
quotes: I feel this pressure, too. Every year. And when I do feel it, I have learned to erase the list and create a new one.

With List 2, the never-finished nature is okay. Of course it's never finished, that list leads us to think, because something as deep and wide as the promotion of long-term human flourishing is always going on.
The meetings aren't the point, the clubs aren't the point, the tests aren't the point, the grades aren't the point. Much of the minutiae does have to get done.
A lot of time, the reason List 1 starts to drive me crazy is because I'm afraid of how I'll look if I don't get it done. What will the teacher down the hall think? What will my boss do?
My reputation is not the point. My ego's desire to be viewed as smart and competent and able to manage it all… not the point. Neither is my job security.

And what this does is it starts to actually make me better at doing List 1. I discern which of the items are just my ego, just my perfectionism. Which are furthest removed from promoting the long-term flourishing of my students?
